paragraphs.text: This is a long essay by Gwern about GPT-3, a text-writing program that OpenAI announced in May 2020. GPT-3 was trained only to guess the next word in a huge pile of internet text. Yet this model, 117 times bigger than GPT-2, could pick up new tasks from just a few examples. The essay calls this "meta-learning": learning how to learn.

sentences.text: This is a long essay by Gwern about GPT-3, a text-writing program that OpenAI announced in May 2020.
GPT-3 was trained only to guess the next word in a huge pile of internet text.
Yet this model, 117 times bigger than GPT-2, could pick up new tasks from just a few examples.
The essay calls this "meta-learning": learning how to learn.

paragraphs.text: Gwern says this matters because it supports the "scaling hypothesis." That is the idea that intelligence is simple learning parts, run at a huge scale. If it is true, making neural networks bigger, with more data and computing power, would keep making them smarter.

paragraphs.text: A key idea is the "blessings of scale": bigger networks learn faster, more steadily, and handle new cases better. GPT-3's gains followed the predicted curves, with no sign yet of slowing down. Gwern also argues that predicting text perfectly would need real understanding, so the last, hardest improvements matter most.

paragraphs.text: The essay says most big AI labs still doubt scaling, and experts who predicted failure were wrong yet rarely admitted it. An appendix warns that AI meant only as a tool may still learn to act like an agent pursuing goals.

fuller.text: This is a long essay by Gwern about GPT-3, an AI system from OpenAI that learned from huge amounts of Internet text. It uses GPT-3 to argue for the scaling hypothesis: the idea that simple neural networks, made much bigger and given more data and computing power, keep getting smarter.

It uses GPT-3 to argue for the scaling hypothesis: the idea that simple neural networks, made much bigger and given more data and computing power, keep getting smarter.

fuller.text: GPT-3 was 117 times larger than GPT-2, its predecessor, yet its gains did not slow down as many expected. It also showed meta-learning, meaning it could pick up a new task from just a few examples in its prompt. Gwern argues the steady scaling curves suggest models with trillions of parameters would be possible and useful.

fuller.text: A key idea is the "blessings of scale": in deep learning, bigger models and harder problems often make learning easier and better. Gwern suggests big models hold countless small sub-models, which average out toward simple, general solutions. He also argues that predicting text nearly as well as humans would require real understanding, so the last bits of error are the deepest.
